Background

Jokowi’s speech in 2014 to the East Asia Summit (EAS) in Naypyidaw, detailed the five underlying pillars of his Maritime policy:

  1. A revival of Indonesia’s maritime culture, recognizing the link between the country’s archipelagic geography, identity, and livelihood;

  2. Improved management of Indonesia’s oceans and fisheries through the development of the country’s fishing industry and building maritime “food sovereignty” and security;

  3. Boosting Indonesia’s maritime economy by improving the country’s port infrastructure, shipping industry, and maritime tourism;

  4. Maritime diplomacy that encourages Indonesia’s partners to work together to eliminate conflict arising over illegal fishing, breaches of sovereignty, territorial disputes, piracy, and environmental concerns like marine pollution; and

  5. Bolstering Indonesia’s maritime defenses, both to support the country’s maritime sovereignty and wealth, and to fulfill its role in maintaining safety of navigation and maritime security.

Funding for the five maritime policy pillars will need to be redirected from other areas of government spending. Jokowi eased some of the budget pressure in late 2014 by cutting domestic fuel subsidies. But while some of the $8 billion saved by raising fuel prices will be available for infrastructure construction, much of it is earmarked for the government’s health, education, and agriculture budgets.

Indonesia’s navy would also need to benefit from a targeted funding boost, as part of a planned increase in overall defense spending to around 1.5 percent of gross domestic product

In spite of the increases in 2012, 2013 and 2014, Indonesia's defence spending was still below 1 per cent of gross domestic product at the end of 2014, much lower than those of almost all its close neighbours.

The MEF programme hinges on Indonesia raising defence spending to this level and to above 2.5 per cent beyond the end of of the second five year plan.

The goal is to build a modern military which is able to deal with any threat across the vast archipelagic state.

The programme is divided into three five-year phases, with the first one completed in 2014 which included the purchase of 163 Leopard tanks from Germany in 2012, the induction of new CN235 PATMAR maritime patrol aircraft and AS-656MBe Panther anti-submarine helicopters. In addition a French-built naval research ship KRI Rigel equipped with an advanced autonomous underwater vehicle was commissioned in late 2014 and 3 submarines recently delivered from South Korea

The second five year plan starts in 2019 and is due for completion by the end of 2023

* Indonesia achieved an average 7.3% per annum growth in GDP from 2015 to 2018 well in excess of the minimum 7% growth required for an increase in the military budget to 1.5% of GDP.
